items.title: Social History
items.summary: Your emergence was always in light blue cotton nightclothes, shuffling already stooped to pick up the paper. You did your primary survey right side, above the fold but no news was good enough; you salvaged the Travel section and threw the rest away, and so it was since your wife died or your hair greyed— I knew no more of your story than this morning ritual, than that you wasted money on a newspaper subscription when you should have bought a Lonely Planet guide.

items.title: “He Lives Alone”: The Social History and Detachment in Poetry and Medicine
items.summary: The poem “Social History” considers how we distance ourselves from others. Although critiques of medical care frequently bemoan unfeeling clinical detachment, here distancing begins outside of the hospital in the very act of observing and then in the writing of the poem itself. The speaker blithely describes a man through the morning ritual she watches: he emerges from his home in “light/blue cotton nightclothes,” retrieves the newspaper, saves the Travel section, discards the rest. items.title: Illicit Injectable Peptides
items.summary: To the Editor Dr Piatkowski and colleagues described how unapproved injectable peptides are promoted for muscle growth, recovery, and antiaging, despite limited human evidence. Janovsky’s observations reinforce our central argument that the rapid expansion of unapproved peptide use is no longer a country-specific regulatory issue, but an increasingly global public health challenge. items.title: Trials of Treatment Deescalation, Deimplementation, and Discontinuation
items.summary: To the Editor As therapeutic options expand and polypharmacy and drug-related harms become increasingly common, evidence-based treatment discontinuation is becoming an important clinical priority. Dr Huang and colleagues’ timely overview of deescalation and discontinuation trials raised a fundamental methodological question: what exactly do these trials estimate?

Yet this framing becomes misleading when body mass index (BMI) is treated as a surrogate for metabolic risk.
